articles.summary: The first wave of enterprise AI was driven by curiosity. Companies experimented, ran pilots and tested what large language models could do. The industry is now shifting to a more demanding phase. Buyers now want measurable returns, finance teams are scrutinizing compute bills, and the businesses gaining ground are those that can show value at a sustainable cost.
articles.title: Enterprise AI Enters Its Economics Phase

articles.summary: For much of the past decade, progress in quantum computing was described in the language of physics: qubit counts, fidelities and coherence times. That vocabulary is giving way to one any infrastructure investor would recognize. Cost per operation, energy, floor space and customer return now set the terms, and the companies best placed for the sector's next phase are already building around them.
articles.title: Quantum Computing Gets Down to Business

articles.summary: Defense has long been one of the hardest industries to enter, with decades-long programs, government customers and high technical barriers. Yet the past four years have produced a wave of new European companies winning contracts and capital at a pace few expected. This shift rests on lasting changes in how wars are fought, how equipment is built and how nations think about their own security.
articles.title: Europe’s Defense Innovators Are Building for the Long Term

articles.summary: European startups raised $42 billion in the first half of 2026, up 50 percent from a year earlier and the strongest stretch for venture funding in four years.[1] The number matters less than what sits behind it: a change in ambition.
articles.title: The New Ambition in European Tech: Key Themes Ahead of Jefferies’ European Disruptive Tech Conference
